questions.title: What Is Garbage Collection in Java? — Reachability and Reference Strengths
questions.question: What is garbage collection in Java? Explain reachability and the different reference strengths.
questions.direct_answer: **Garbage collection** is the JVM's automatic process of reclaiming memory used by objects no longer **reachable** from any **GC root** (active threads, static fields, JNI references, the stack). **Reachability** — not reference count — decides eligibility, which is why circular references are collected correctly. Java exposes four reference strengths: **strong** (default, prevents collection), **soft** (collected only under memory pressure, useful for caches), **weak** (collected at the next GC, used in WeakHashMap and ThreadLocal), and **phantom** (used for cleanup notification after finalization).

sections.title: GC Frees You from manual `free()` — But Not from Memory Leaks
sections.content:
Java's garbage collector exists for one reason: in C and C++, every `malloc` requires a matching `free`, and getting that wrong produces use-after-free crashes, double-free corruption, or slow leaks that bring down long-running services. Java eliminates this entire class of bugs by making the JVM responsible for reclaiming memory. You allocate with `new`, and the GC decides when (and whether) to free.

The core mechanism is **reachability tracing**. The GC starts from a fixed set of **GC roots** — currently executing thread stacks, static fields of loaded classes, JNI references held by native code, and the system class loader — and walks every reference it can follow. Anything reachable is live; anything unreachable is garbage. This is fundamentally different from reference counting (used by Python's CPython and Objective-C ARC), which increments a counter on every assignment and frees when the count hits zero. Reference counting cannot reclaim **circular references** without extra cycle-detection logic. Tracing collectors handle circular references for free: if neither object in a cycle is reachable from a GC root, both are collected.

This matters because Java developers often assume "GC means no memory leaks." That is wrong. **A leak in Java is anything reachable that you no longer need** — typically static collections that grow forever, event listeners that are never unregistered, or thread-local values that outlive their thread. The GC will not collect any of these because they are still reachable from a root. Understanding reachability is what separates someone who knows GC exists from someone who can debug a production memory leak.

sections.title: The Four Reference Strengths and When to Use Each
sections.content:
Java provides four levels of reference strength through the `java.lang.ref` package. Each tells the GC how aggressively to reclaim the referent.

| Reference Type | When Collected | Typical Use Case |
|---|---|---|
| Strong (default) | Never while reachable | All normal object references — `String s = "hello"` |
| `SoftReference` | Only under memory pressure | Memory-sensitive caches that the JVM may shrink |
| `WeakReference` | At the next GC if no strong refs exist | `WeakHashMap` keys, `ThreadLocal` entries, listener registries |
| `PhantomReference` | After finalization, before reclamation | Cleanup notification (replaces `finalize()`) — `Cleaner` API |

**Strong references** are the default — every `=` assignment creates one, and they pin the object in memory until they go out of scope. **Soft references** survive until the JVM is about to throw `OutOfMemoryError`; the GC then clears them to reclaim space. They sound ideal for caches but in practice often perform worse than a bounded cache like Caffeine because softly referenced objects survive far longer than their last useful access.

**Weak references** are the workhorse for breaking unwanted retention. `WeakHashMap` uses weak keys so that when the only remaining reference to a key is the map's own entry, the entry becomes eligible for collection. This pattern is essential for caches keyed by class objects (avoids ClassLoader leaks) and for listener registries that should not prevent listeners from being garbage collected. **Phantom references** are rarely written by application code directly; they exist to support the modern `Cleaner` API, which replaces the deprecated `finalize()` method for native resource cleanup.

sections.title: Reachability in Practice — The Code That Reveals Each Reference Type
The Real Memory-Leak Patterns That Survive GC
sections.content:
Garbage collection eliminates several classes of bugs but not memory leaks themselves. Knowing which patterns leak in Java despite GC is far more interview-relevant than knowing the GC algorithm.

**Patterns that leak through reachability:**
- **Static collections that grow forever** — a `static Map<String, User> CACHE` that never evicts will eventually fill the heap. Use a bounded cache (Caffeine, Guava) or `WeakHashMap` keyed appropriately.
- **Listener registrations that are never removed** — registering `addPropertyChangeListener` and never calling `removeListener` creates strong references from the publisher to the subscriber, often pinning entire UI graphs or HTTP request scopes.
- **`ThreadLocal` in pooled threads** — values set on a thread-local in a Tomcat or ForkJoinPool worker thread persist for the life of the thread. Always `remove()` in a `finally` block.
- **Inner classes capturing enclosing instances** — a non-static inner class implicitly holds a reference to its outer class. If you stash an `OuterClass.InnerListener` in a static registry, you've pinned the entire `OuterClass` graph in memory.
- **ClassLoader leaks** — a single static reference from an undeployed web application's ClassLoader prevents the entire classloader (and all its loaded classes and static fields) from being collected. The classic Tomcat hot-redeploy memory leak.

**Patterns that GC handles automatically:**
- **Circular object graphs** — A → B → A is collected because tracing starts from roots, not from references between objects.
- **Local variables going out of scope** — collected at the next eligible GC.
- **Large temporary allocations** — minor GC reclaims short-lived objects in milliseconds; this is what generational GC is optimized for.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **GC is tracing, not reference counting** — walks from GC roots; circular references are collected for free.
- **GC roots include thread stacks, static fields, JNI references, and the system class loader** — anything reachable from these is live.
- **Strong references are the default** — created by every `=` assignment; pin objects in memory.
- **Soft references** — cleared only under memory pressure; useful but often outperformed by bounded caches.
- **Weak references** — cleared at the next GC; the basis for `WeakHashMap` and proper `ThreadLocal` cleanup.
- **Phantom references** — for cleanup notification; powers the modern `Cleaner` API replacing `finalize()`.
- **GC does not prevent memory leaks** — static collections, unremoved listeners, and `ThreadLocal` in pooled threads still leak.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java's garbage collector automatically reclaims memory used by objects no longer reachable from the application. The key insight is that GC is **reachability-based**, not reference-count-based — it starts from a set of GC roots like thread stacks and static fields, and any object it cannot reach is garbage.

**How GC decides what's garbage:**
- Walks references from GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references, system class loader
- Anything unreachable is collected — including circular reference cycles, which reference counting cannot handle
- This is why Java does not need explicit `free()` calls and why circular references do not leak

**Reference strengths from strongest to weakest:**
- **Strong** — the default `=` assignment; pins objects in memory until they go out of scope
- **Soft** — collected only under memory pressure; designed for caches but often worse than bounded caches like Caffeine
- **Weak** — collected at the next GC; powers `WeakHashMap` and `ThreadLocal` cleanup
- **Phantom** — used for cleanup notification after finalization; backs the modern `Cleaner` API

**Common misconception to address:**
- GC does not prevent all memory leaks — it only collects unreachable objects
- The most common Java memory leaks are: static collections that grow forever, listener registrations that are never removed, and `ThreadLocal` values in pooled threads

In an interview, I'd emphasize that understanding reachability is what lets you debug a production heap dump — knowing the GC algorithm is secondary.

questions.title: Generational Garbage Collection — Young vs Old Generation Explained
questions.question: Explain generational garbage collection in Java. What are Eden, Survivor spaces, and the Tenured generation, and how does promotion work?
questions.direct_answer: **Generational GC** splits the heap into **young** (Eden + Survivor) and **old** generations because most objects die young. **Minor GC** collects only the young generation — fast, frequent pauses. **Major/full GC** collects the old generation (and often the whole heap) — slower, rarer. Objects survive a configurable number of minor collections (**tenuring threshold**) before promotion to old.

sections.title: The Weak Generational Hypothesis Is Why GC Can Be Fast
sections.content:
Empirical analysis of object lifetimes in real applications consistently shows the same shape: the vast majority of objects die very young. Local variables, intermediate calculation results, request-scoped DTOs, parser tokens, JSON-deserialized fields — these account for most allocation but are unreachable within milliseconds. A small minority — caches, application configuration, long-lived business objects — survive much longer. This pattern is the **weak generational hypothesis**, and it is the single most important optimization in modern garbage collectors.

If the GC had to scan the entire heap every time it wanted to reclaim memory, the cost would scale with **live data size**, not with garbage produced. By splitting the heap into a small **young generation** (typically 30-40% of the heap) and a larger **old generation**, the JVM can collect just the young generation frequently — a process called **minor GC** — and only touch the old generation when necessary in a **major** or **full GC**. Because most objects in the young generation are dead, minor GC is fast: it copies the few survivors elsewhere and reclaims the entire region at once.

This split also enables better cache locality (recently allocated objects sit together in Eden), simpler allocation (just a bump-the-pointer in Eden), and fewer write barriers during normal execution. The cost is the bookkeeping needed to track references from old generation back into young generation — known as the **remembered set** or **card table** — but this overhead is small compared to the savings from not scanning the entire heap on every GC.

sections.title: The Layout: Eden, Survivor, and Tenured
sections.content:
The young generation is not one big region. It is split into three smaller areas, each with a distinct role in the copy-collect mechanism.

| Region | Default Size Ratio | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Eden | ~80% of young gen | All new allocations land here |
| Survivor 0 (S0) | ~10% of young gen | Holds objects that survived 1+ minor GCs |
| Survivor 1 (S1) | ~10% of young gen | Holds the *other* survivor cohort (only one is active at a time) |
| Tenured (Old Gen) | Configurable, often 60-70% of heap | Long-lived objects promoted from young gen |

**Eden** is where `new` allocates. Allocation is essentially a pointer bump — the JVM increments a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB) pointer and returns the previous value. This is faster than `malloc` precisely because there is no free-list management; Eden is treated as a contiguous bump region until it fills.

When Eden fills, a **minor GC** triggers. The collector identifies live objects in Eden and the active Survivor space (say S0), copies them to the empty Survivor space (S1), and clears Eden and S0 in one shot. The roles of S0 and S1 swap on the next cycle. This **copying collector** design — based on the classic Cheney's algorithm — is why minor GC is fast: the work is proportional to the **live** data, not the total Eden size, and the entire region is reclaimed wholesale rather than in fragments.

**Promotion** to the old generation happens when an object's age (incremented each time it survives a minor GC) reaches the **tenuring threshold** — `-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold`, default 15 in HotSpot. The JVM also dynamically lowers this threshold if the Survivor space is overflowing, which is when problems start.

sections.title: What Happens During a Minor GC — Step by Step
sections.content:
Tracing through a single minor GC cycle illustrates how the regions interact and where the cost goes.

**1. Allocation fills Eden.** Application threads call `new` and bump the Eden pointer. When Eden has no more room for a request, the allocating thread triggers a minor GC.

**2. Stop-the-world begins.** All application threads pause at the next safepoint. This is the visible pause time — typically 5-50ms depending on heap size and live data.

**3. Reachability scan.** The collector scans GC roots (thread stacks, static fields, JNI references) plus the **remembered set** that tracks any old-to-young references. It marks every reachable object in Eden and the active Survivor space.

**4. Copy survivors.** Live objects are copied to the empty Survivor space (or directly to old gen if their age has reached the tenuring threshold). The age in each object's header is incremented. References to copied objects are updated.

**5. Clear Eden and the source Survivor.** Both are now empty. Eden is reset to a bump-pointer. Application threads resume.

A crucial detail: **if the Survivor space cannot hold all the survivors**, they are promoted directly to the old generation regardless of age. This **premature promotion** is one of the most important GC pathologies to understand. It manifests as old generation filling up much faster than expected, which triggers more frequent (and far more expensive) major GCs.

Diagnostic flags for production:

```bash
# Show survivor distribution and tenuring distribution per minor GC
-XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution

# Tune the survivor ratio if survivors regularly overflow
-XX:SurvivorRatio=8     # Eden:S0:S1 = 8:1:1 (default)
-XX:NewRatio=2          # Old:Young = 2:1 (default)

# Adjust the tenuring threshold
-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold=15
```

In GC logs, look for `Desired survivor size` versus actual survivor occupancy. If actual is consistently larger than desired, you are losing the generational benefit.

sections.title: When Generational GC Helps — and When It Hurts
sections.content:
Generational GC is a near-universal win, but the design assumes the weak generational hypothesis holds. Workloads that violate it pay an overhead penalty without getting the benefit.

**Workloads where generational GC excels:**
- **Web services** — request-scoped objects (DTOs, JSON nodes, SQL parameter holders) die within milliseconds; the young generation reclaims them efficiently.
- **Stream processing** — short-lived events flow through the pipeline; survivors are rare.
- **Compilation, parsing, and serialization** — produces large amounts of short-lived intermediate state.

**Workloads where generational GC underperforms:**
- **Large in-memory caches** — most allocations are intended to survive; objects move through young gen wastefully before promoting. Consider a non-generational collector like ZGC or sizing the young generation small.
- **Bulk allocation of large objects** — objects above a threshold (`PretenureSizeThreshold` in some collectors) bypass young gen entirely and go straight to old, which can fragment it.
- **Object pooling** — reusing objects defeats the generational model because pooled objects keep getting touched, never aging out of cycles. Modern GCs are fast enough that pooling is usually counterproductive.

**The pathology to watch for in production:** **promotion failure**. If the old generation has no room to accept survivors during a minor GC, the JVM falls back to a full GC — and that full GC stops all threads for seconds. In G1 specifically, this manifests as `to-space exhausted` events in the GC log. The fix is usually increasing `-Xmx`, increasing `-XX:G1ReservePercent`, or finding the leak that is filling the old generation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Weak generational hypothesis** — most objects die young; the foundation of generational GC.
- **Young generation layout** — Eden (~80%), S0 (~10%), S1 (~10%); only one Survivor is active at a time.
- **Minor GC** — copies survivors from Eden + active Survivor to the empty Survivor; reclaims the rest.
- **Tenuring threshold** — `-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold` (default 15); object's age increments on each surviving GC.
- **Promotion to old generation** — happens when age hits threshold or when Survivor cannot hold all survivors (premature promotion).
- **Premature promotion is the #1 generational GC pathology** — fills old gen faster than expected, triggering expensive major/full GCs.
- **Diagnose with `-XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution`** — shows whether Survivor sizing matches your allocation pattern.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Generational garbage collection is built on a single empirical observation called the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. The JVM exploits this by splitting the heap into a young generation, where new objects live briefly, and an old generation for long-lived objects.

**Young generation layout:**
- **Eden** (about 80% of young gen) — where every `new` allocation lands
- **Survivor 0** and **Survivor 1** (about 10% each) — only one is active at a time; the other stays empty as the copy target

**Minor GC mechanics:**
- Triggered when Eden fills
- Live objects in Eden and the active Survivor are copied to the empty Survivor
- Eden and the source Survivor are reclaimed in one shot — fast because most of the young gen is dead
- The roles of S0 and S1 swap each cycle

**Promotion to old generation:**
- Each object has an age in its header, incremented each time it survives a minor GC
- When age hits `-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold` (default 15), the object is promoted to old gen
- If the Survivor space cannot hold all survivors, they are **prematurely promoted** to old gen regardless of age — this is the main GC pathology to watch for

**Why this design is fast:**
- Minor GC cost scales with live data, not Eden size
- Bump-pointer allocation in Eden is faster than `malloc`
- Old generation is collected far less frequently because it grows slowly

In an interview, I'd emphasize that **diagnosing premature promotion** with `-XX:+PrintTenuringDistribution` is more practical knowledge than memorizing the default ratios.

sections.title: Every Collector Makes a Different Bet on the Throughput-vs-Latency Spectrum
sections.content:
Choosing a garbage collector is not about finding the "best" one — it is about matching the collector's design trade-off to your workload's requirements. **Parallel GC** bets everything on throughput by stopping all application threads for collection, accepting multi-second pauses. **G1GC** aims for a middle ground, dividing the heap into regions and collecting the most garbage-dense regions first to meet a configurable pause-time target. **ZGC** and **Shenandoah** push pause times below one millisecond by performing nearly all GC work concurrently with application threads, at the cost of higher CPU overhead.

The trap is assuming newer always means better. ZGC achieves remarkable pause times, but it uses more CPU for its concurrent work and more memory for its colored pointer metadata. For a batch processing job that cares only about total execution time, Parallel GC outperforms every concurrent collector. For a Spring Boot web service with moderate latency requirements, G1GC (the default since Java 9) handles the job with minimal tuning.

**CMS** (Concurrent Mark Sweep) held the low-pause role before G1 but was removed in Java 14 due to fragmentation issues and maintenance burden. Any production system still referencing CMS should migrate to G1 or ZGC.

sections.title: Selecting a Garbage Collector
sections.content:
```bash
# G1 — default for services (Java 9+)
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 -jar app.jar

# ZGC — sub-ms pauses, large heaps
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx16g -jar app.jar

# Parallel — batch throughput
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -jar batch.jar
```

Interviewers expect a short runnable snippet plus one failure case — not pseudocode.

sections.title: Head-to-Head: Pause Time, Throughput, and When to Switch
sections.content:
The following comparison captures the essential selection criteria. The right choice depends on your latency SLA, heap size, and whether you can afford the CPU overhead of concurrent collection.

| Collector | Pause Time | Throughput | Default In | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parallel GC | Seconds (multi-thread STW) | Highest | Java 8 | Batch jobs, offline processing |
| G1GC | 100-200ms target | High | Java 9+ | General web services, 4GB+ heaps |
| ZGC | Sub-millisecond | High (more CPU) | — | Latency-critical APIs, large heaps |
| Shenandoah | Sub-millisecond | Moderate | — | Low-pause alternative (Red Hat JDK) |

**G1GC** works by dividing the heap into equal-sized regions (1-32MB) and tracking how much live data each region contains. During a pause, it evacuates the regions with the most garbage first — hence "Garbage-First." The `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` flag sets a soft target that G1 tries to meet by adjusting how many regions it collects per cycle. This region-based approach also eliminates the fragmentation problems that plagued CMS.

**ZGC** uses colored pointers and load barriers to relocate objects concurrently. Application threads see a consistent heap view because every pointer load passes through a barrier that updates references transparently. The trade-off is roughly 5-15% additional CPU overhead and approximately 3% memory overhead for the pointer metadata. For heaps under 4GB where pause times are already short with G1, the CPU cost of ZGC provides no net benefit.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Parallel GC** — highest throughput; stop-the-world pauses can last seconds; for batch processing only.
- **G1GC (default Java 9+)** — region-based; soft pause-time target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`; good for web services.
- **ZGC** — sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size; higher CPU usage for concurrent collection work.
- **Shenandoah** — similar goals to ZGC; different algorithm; available in OpenJDK.
- **ZGC is not universally better** — on small heaps under 4GB, G1 pauses are already short; ZGC's CPU overhead provides no benefit.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java ships with four main garbage collectors, each making a different trade-off between throughput, pause duration, and CPU overhead. There is no universally best choice — the right GC algorithm depends on what your application can tolerate: long pauses for high throughput, or short pauses at higher CPU cost.

**Parallel GC:**
- Highest throughput — throws all threads at collection during stop-the-world pauses
- Pauses can last seconds — suitable for batch processing and offline analytics, not for user-facing services

**G1GC (default since Java 9):**
- Region-based heap — collects regions with the highest garbage ratio first
- Soft pause-time target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200`; adjusts collection scope to meet it
- Avoids fragmentation issues that killed CMS; good default for most web services

**ZGC:**
- Almost all work done concurrently with application threads — sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size
- Higher CPU usage for concurrent GC work
- Use when even 200ms pauses are unacceptable: algorithmic trading, real-time pricing, strict p99 SLAs

**Common mistake:**
- Assuming ZGC is universally better — on small heaps under 4GB, G1 pauses are already short; ZGC's CPU overhead provides no net benefit

I recommend G1 as the default, enabling GC logging, and only switching if p99 latency analysis shows GC pauses as the dominant contributor.

sections.title: CMS Made Pauses Short by Sacrificing Compaction — That Was Its Fatal Flaw
sections.content:
**CMS (Concurrent Mark Sweep)** was Java's first major attempt at a low-pause garbage collector. Its core insight was that the **mark** phase — identifying live objects — could be done concurrently with application threads, leaving only short stop-the-world pauses for the **sweep** (reclamation) of unreachable memory. For workloads with strict pause-time requirements in the early 2010s, CMS was a transformative improvement over the throughput-focused Parallel GC.

But CMS made one design decision that would ultimately doom it: **it never compacts the old generation**. Sweeping reclaimed the memory of dead objects in place, leaving a free list of fragmented holes. Over time, fragmentation made it impossible to allocate large contiguous objects in the old generation — even when there was technically enough free memory. When this happened, CMS fell back to a **single-threaded, stop-the-world serial full GC** that compacted the entire heap. These full GCs could last tens of seconds, completely defeating the point of using a low-pause collector.

**G1GC** was Oracle's answer. Instead of treating the heap as one contiguous old generation, G1 divides it into hundreds or thousands of equal-sized **regions** (1-32MB each). Each region can be Eden, Survivor, Old, or Humongous (for very large objects). G1 tracks how much garbage each region contains and evacuates the highest-garbage regions first — that is the "garbage first" of the name. Crucially, **G1 compacts as it evacuates**: live objects are copied to fresh regions, old regions are reclaimed wholesale, and fragmentation is eliminated as a side effect of normal collection.

G1 was made the default GC in Java 9, CMS was deprecated in the same release, and CMS was removed entirely in Java 14. The official rationale: maintaining two complex concurrent collectors was a burden, G1 had reached feature parity with CMS, and CMS's fragmentation issues had proved unfixable.

sections.title: G1 vs CMS — Architecture and Operational Differences
sections.content:
The two collectors share a goal (low pause times) but differ in nearly every implementation detail.

| Dimension | CMS | G1GC |
|---|---|---|
| Heap layout | Traditional contiguous young/old | Hundreds of equal-sized regions |
| Compaction | None (sweep only) | Incremental during evacuation |
| Pause-time target | No soft target — use heuristics | `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` (soft target) |
| Fragmentation | Major problem; triggers serial full GC | Eliminated by region evacuation |
| Concurrent-mode failure | Falls back to single-threaded full GC | No equivalent — incremental work continues |
| Tuning complexity | Many interdependent flags | Pause target + heap size; minimal tuning |
| Status | Removed in Java 14 | Default since Java 9 |
| Best for (historical) | Latency-sensitive, heaps under 4GB | All general workloads, 4GB+ heaps |

**Concurrent-mode failure** is the CMS pathology to know. CMS starts a concurrent mark cycle when the old generation reaches a threshold (`-XX:CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction`, default 92% in later versions). If the application allocates faster than CMS can free, the old generation fills before the concurrent cycle completes — and the JVM falls back to a serial, single-threaded full GC that can take tens of seconds. Tuning around this required guessing the right initiating threshold and accepting that the GC could fail at any time.

**G1's region-based design** sidesteps this entirely. There is no all-or-nothing concurrent cycle — G1 collects a few regions per pause, and if it falls behind, it simply collects more regions per cycle. The soft pause-time target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` lets the GC choose how much work to do per pause, balancing latency against the rate of memory reclamation.

sections.title: Migrating from CMS to G1 — The Practical Steps
sections.content:
If you are running an older service still configured for CMS, the migration to G1 is straightforward but requires testing, especially for heap sizing and pause-time targets.

**1. Replace CMS flags with G1 flags.** A typical CMS configuration looked like this:

```bash
-XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC \
-XX:+CMSParallelRemarkEnabled \
-XX:CMSInitiatingOccupancyFraction=70 \
-XX:+UseCMSInitiatingOccupancyOnly \
-XX:+ScavengeBeforeFullGC
```

The equivalent G1 configuration is dramatically simpler:

```bash
-XX:+UseG1GC \
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \
-Xmx8g -Xms8g \
-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m
```

**2. Size the heap generously.** G1 needs more headroom than CMS — Oracle recommends roughly 10-20% more heap to maintain similar pause times. The benefit is no concurrent-mode failures and no serial full GCs.

**3. Set a realistic pause-time target.** `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` is the default. Lower values (e.g., 50ms) cause G1 to collect smaller chunks per cycle, which means more total CPU spent on GC — a throughput penalty for the pause-time benefit.

**4. Monitor `humongous` allocations.** Objects larger than half a region size become **humongous objects** allocated directly into old gen, bypassing young gen entirely. They can fragment region allocation and cause early major GC. The diagnostic is in the GC log: look for `Humongous Reclaim` events. If you see many, increase region size with `-XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m` (must be a power of 2, between 1MB and 32MB).

**5. Validate p99 latency in load testing.** G1 pauses are usually shorter and more predictable than CMS, but the distribution differs — there is no concurrent-mode-failure long tail, but average pause may be slightly longer. Compare apples-to-apples with a realistic production-shape load test before flipping the switch.

sections.title: What G1 Gives Up — Honest Trade-Offs vs CMS
sections.content:
G1 is the right choice for almost every modern workload, but it is not strictly superior on every dimension. Understanding what G1 sacrifices makes you a more credible engineer.

**What G1 does better than CMS:**
- **No fragmentation** — incremental compaction means no concurrent-mode failures, no serial full GC.
- **Predictable pause times** — soft target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis`; the JVM adjusts collection scope to meet it.
- **Simpler tuning** — a handful of flags vs CMS's dozens.
- **Better diagnostics** — Java 9+ unified GC logging is far more readable.

**Where CMS sometimes had an edge (historically):**
- **Lower average pause on small heaps** — for heaps under 4GB with steady allocation patterns, CMS pauses could be slightly shorter.
- **Lower CPU overhead** — G1's remembered set maintenance and write barriers cost a few percent more CPU.
- **More predictable young GC pause** — G1's mixed collections can occasionally produce longer pauses than a pure CMS young GC.

**The verdict:** none of CMS's advantages outweigh the risk of concurrent-mode failure. A single 30-second serial full GC in production destroys SLAs in a way that no average-pause improvement can compensate for. This is why Oracle removed CMS rather than maintain it as a legacy option.

**For latency below G1's reach** — single-digit-millisecond pauses on multi-gigabyte heaps — the modern answer is **ZGC** or **Shenandoah**, not CMS. Both achieve sub-millisecond pauses by performing nearly all work concurrently, including compaction, at the cost of additional CPU overhead.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CMS = Concurrent Mark Sweep** — concurrent mark, no compaction, fragments old gen over time.
- **G1 = Garbage First** — region-based heap; evacuates highest-garbage regions first; compacts incrementally.
- **Concurrent-mode failure** — CMS's fatal flaw; fragmentation forces a serial single-threaded full GC.
- **G1 has no equivalent failure mode** — incremental work continues even under pressure.
- **G1 is default since Java 9** — CMS deprecated in Java 9, removed in Java 14.
- **G1 needs 10-20% more heap than CMS** — for similar pause times.
- **Soft pause-time target** — `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` is unique to G1; CMS had no equivalent.
- **For sub-millisecond pauses** — use ZGC or Shenandoah, not CMS.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
G1GC and CMS were both designed to reduce GC pause times compared to Parallel GC, but they took different architectural approaches — and CMS's choices ultimately led to its deprecation in Java 9 and removal in Java 14.

**CMS — Concurrent Mark Sweep:**
- Marks live objects concurrently with application threads — short stop-the-world pauses for marking phases
- Sweeps in place — does not compact the old generation
- Fragmentation builds up over time, eventually causing **concurrent-mode failure**
- When that happens, the JVM falls back to a single-threaded serial full GC that can take tens of seconds

**G1GC — Garbage First:**
- Divides the heap into hundreds of equal-sized regions (1-32MB each)
- Tracks garbage density per region; evacuates the highest-garbage regions first
- **Compacts incrementally** during evacuation — no fragmentation
- Soft pause-time target via `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` — unique to G1; CMS had no equivalent

**Why CMS was removed:**
- Concurrent-mode failures were impossible to fully prevent and produced multi-second pauses that defeated the point of using a low-pause GC
- Maintaining two complex concurrent collectors was a burden on the OpenJDK team
- G1 had reached feature parity and offered better predictability

**Migration practicalities:**
- Replace `-XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC` with `-XX:+UseG1GC`
- Increase heap size by 10-20% — G1 needs more headroom
- Set a realistic pause-time target — lower values trade throughput for shorter pauses
- Monitor humongous allocations in the GC log

**For modern low-latency needs**, the answer is ZGC or Shenandoah — both achieve sub-millisecond pauses by performing nearly all work concurrently.

questions.title: ZGC and Shenandoah — Sub-Millisecond Pauses Through Concurrent Compaction
questions.question: How do ZGC and Shenandoah achieve sub-millisecond GC pauses? What are the trade-offs and when should you use them?
questions.direct_answer: ZGC and Shenandoah achieve sub-millisecond pauses by performing **all** GC work — including compaction — concurrently with application threads. ZGC (Oracle, production-ready in Java 15) uses **colored pointers** and load barriers to relocate objects without stopping the world. Shenandoah (Red Hat, production-ready in Java 15) uses **Brooks pointers** (forwarding pointers in object headers) for the same goal. Both target heaps from a few hundred MB to multiple TB with pauses under 10ms — and typically under 1ms. The trade-off is 5-15% additional CPU overhead and modest extra memory for the relocation metadata. Use them when p99 latency requirements are stricter than what G1's `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` can deliver.

sections.title: Concurrent Compaction Is the Hard Problem That ZGC and Shenandoah Solve
sections.content:
Every garbage collector before ZGC and Shenandoah faced the same wall: **compaction must stop application threads**. You cannot move an object while another thread is reading from it without risk of corruption. CMS sidestepped this by never compacting (and paid the price in fragmentation). G1 compacts incrementally but still requires a stop-the-world pause to evacuate each region. As heap sizes grew from gigabytes to terabytes, even G1's 200ms pauses became unacceptable for latency-critical workloads.

**ZGC and Shenandoah solve concurrent compaction** through different mechanisms but with the same core idea: insert a small piece of indirection — a **read barrier** or **load barrier** — into every reference load, so the runtime can transparently redirect access to a moved object. With this barrier in place, the GC can relocate objects in the background without coordinating with application threads. Pauses are reduced to short root-scanning steps that scale with the number of threads, **not the heap size**. This is the breakthrough: ZGC pause times are roughly the same on a 1GB heap as on a 16TB heap.

**ZGC** uses **colored pointers** — extra metadata bits embedded directly in 64-bit references — to encode the GC state of an object (marked, remapped, finalizable, etc.). The load barrier checks these bits on every pointer load and triggers GC bookkeeping when needed. **Shenandoah** uses **Brooks pointers** — a forwarding pointer in every object header that points to the object's current location. Both designs achieve the same end goal: the application thread reads through the indirection and accesses the correct memory address, while the GC works in the background.

The trade-off is real: load barriers cost a few percent of CPU on every pointer load, and concurrent collection requires sustained background CPU work. For an application that already meets its latency SLA with G1, switching to ZGC just costs CPU without delivering benefit. ZGC is the right choice when even G1's tail pauses violate the SLA.

sections.title: ZGC vs Shenandoah vs G1 — When to Use Each
sections.content:
All three are concurrent collectors, but they target different design points.

| Dimension | G1GC | ZGC | Shenandoah |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pause time target | 100-200ms | <1ms (typically <100µs) | <10ms (typically <1ms) |
| Pause scales with | Heap size (mixed collections) | **Number of threads** (root scan only) | **Number of threads** (root scan only) |
| Heap size sweet spot | 4GB - 64GB | 8MB - 16TB | 100MB - 4TB |
| Concurrent compaction | No (incremental during STW) | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| Indirection mechanism | None | Colored pointers + load barrier | Brooks pointer + load barrier |
| Generational support | Yes (always) | Yes (Java 21+) | Yes (Java 24+) |
| CPU overhead | Low | 5-15% | 5-15% |
| Memory overhead | ~5% | ~3% (colored pointer metadata) | ~5-10% (forwarding pointers) |
| Vendor | Oracle / OpenJDK | Oracle / OpenJDK | Red Hat / OpenJDK |
| Default in | Java 9+ | — | — |
| Production-ready since | Java 9 | Java 15 | Java 15 |

**ZGC** is the right choice for the largest heaps and the strictest latency requirements. Its pause-time guarantees are remarkable: typically **under 100 microseconds** regardless of heap size, with worst-case pauses under 1 millisecond. The trade-off is roughly 5-15% additional CPU overhead and the requirement that the workload tolerate a few percent throughput reduction.

**Shenandoah** has similar goals to ZGC and is the natural choice in Red Hat-supported environments. It was developed independently and uses a different relocation algorithm (Brooks forwarding pointers vs ZGC's colored pointers), but the operational characteristics are similar. Choose Shenandoah on Red Hat's OpenJDK distributions; choose ZGC on Oracle's or Adoptium's.

**G1GC** remains the right default for general workloads. If your p99 latency analysis shows GC as a small contributor relative to other sources (database calls, downstream services, lock contention), the CPU cost of ZGC delivers no business value. Switch to ZGC when GC pauses are demonstrably the dominant tail latency contributor.

sections.title: How ZGC Performs Concurrent Compaction — The Colored Pointer Trick
sections.content:
Understanding ZGC's mechanism makes it click why the pause time is independent of heap size. The key is that ZGC encodes GC state directly in 64-bit pointer values rather than in the object headers.

**The colored pointer.** A 64-bit pointer in ZGC uses several high bits as **color bits** — currently `Marked0`, `Marked1`, `Remapped`, and `Finalizable`. The address bits remain in the lower 44 bits, giving access to up to 16TB of heap. Every pointer load passes through a **load barrier** that checks these color bits. If the bits indicate the object has moved or needs marking, the barrier performs the bookkeeping inline, transparent to application code.

**The five concurrent phases:**

1. **Pause Mark Start** (microseconds, STW) — scan thread stacks and mark roots reachable from the stack.
2. **Concurrent Mark/Remap** — application threads run; load barriers triggered by stale pointers cause incremental marking and pointer fixup.
3. **Pause Mark End** (microseconds, STW) — finalize the mark phase by re-scanning roots.
4. **Concurrent Prepare for Relocation** — choose which regions to evacuate based on garbage density.
5. **Concurrent Relocate** — copy live objects from chosen regions to new regions while application threads continue running. The load barrier ensures application threads always see the current location.

No phase requires all application threads to be stopped while the heap is scanned. The only stop-the-world work is the brief root-scanning at the boundaries of mark phases, which scales with the **number of threads**, not the heap size. This is why ZGC pauses do not grow when the heap goes from 1GB to 16TB.

**Configuration is minimal.** Enabling ZGC requires:

```bash
-XX:+UseZGC \
-Xmx16g \
-Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags
```

For Java 21+, generational ZGC is opt-in (and is becoming default in Java 23+):

```bash
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational
```

Non-generational ZGC paid a throughput penalty because it scanned the entire heap on every cycle. Generational ZGC adds the weak generational hypothesis to ZGC's concurrent design, dramatically reducing the work per cycle and closing the throughput gap with G1.

sections.title: When Sub-Millisecond Pauses Are Worth the CPU Cost
sections.content:
ZGC and Shenandoah are not free. Knowing when their cost is justified by the latency benefit is the difference between a senior engineer and someone who just chases the latest features.

**Use cases that justify ZGC or Shenandoah:**
- **Algorithmic trading** — even 200ms pauses cause missed market opportunities; sub-millisecond pauses are mandatory.
- **Real-time bidding (ad tech)** — bid responses have hard 100ms deadlines from request to response.
- **High-frequency telemetry pipelines** — tail latency directly affects observability and downstream alerting.
- **Very large heaps (>32GB)** — G1's pause time scales with heap size; ZGC's does not.
- **Latency-sensitive APIs with strict p99 SLAs** — when GC is the dominant tail latency contributor and other sources have been optimized.

**Use cases where ZGC is overkill:**
- **Standard web services with p99 < 1 second SLAs** — G1's 200ms target is well within budget; the CPU cost of ZGC delivers no business value.
- **Batch processing and offline analytics** — total throughput matters more than latency; Parallel GC is faster.
- **Heaps under 4GB** — G1 pauses are already short on small heaps; ZGC's overhead provides no benefit.
- **CPU-bound workloads** — the additional 5-15% CPU overhead of ZGC may push you over capacity.

**The diagnostic process** before switching collectors:

1. Measure current p99 latency and decompose it: how much is GC, how much is network, how much is downstream service calls, how much is lock contention?
2. Enable detailed GC logging on G1 and capture pause distribution.
3. If GC is the dominant tail contributor, calculate the budget improvement from sub-millisecond pauses.
4. Run a load test with ZGC enabled and measure both latency improvement and throughput cost.
5. Decide based on the actual trade-off in your workload, not on benchmarks from other systems.

sections.content:
- **Concurrent compaction** is the breakthrough — both ZGC and Shenandoah relocate objects while application threads run.
- **ZGC** uses **colored pointers** (metadata bits in 64-bit references) and load barriers; Oracle/OpenJDK; production-ready Java 15+.
- **Shenandoah** uses **Brooks pointers** (forwarding pointers in object headers); Red Hat/OpenJDK; production-ready Java 15+.
- **Pause time is independent of heap size** — scales with number of threads (root scan only); typically <1ms.
- **CPU overhead is real** — 5-15% extra for the load barrier and concurrent relocation work.
- **Generational ZGC** (Java 21+) closed the throughput gap by exploiting the weak generational hypothesis.
- **G1 is still the default** for general workloads; switch only when GC is the dominant tail latency contributor.
- **Use cases** — algorithmic trading, real-time bidding, very large heaps (>32GB), strict p99 SLAs.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
ZGC and Shenandoah achieve sub-millisecond pause times by solving the hardest problem in garbage collection: **concurrent compaction**. Every collector before them required stopping application threads to safely move objects in memory. ZGC and Shenandoah eliminate that requirement using load barriers and pointer indirection.

**The core mechanism:**
- A small read barrier — a few CPU instructions — runs on every pointer load
- The barrier transparently redirects reads to the current location of moved objects
- The GC can relocate objects in the background while the application keeps running

**ZGC specifically:**
- Uses **colored pointers** — extra metadata bits embedded in 64-bit references
- The load barrier checks these bits and triggers GC bookkeeping when needed
- Pauses scale with the number of threads, not heap size — same pause on 1GB and 16TB heaps
- Production-ready since Java 15; generational ZGC since Java 21 closed the throughput gap

**Shenandoah specifically:**
- Uses **Brooks pointers** — a forwarding pointer in every object header
- Similar pause-time characteristics to ZGC; different algorithm; Red Hat's choice

**Trade-offs to be honest about:**
- 5-15% additional CPU overhead for the load barrier and concurrent work
- Modest memory overhead — about 3% for ZGC's colored pointer metadata
- For workloads where G1 already meets the SLA, ZGC just costs CPU without business value

**When to choose them:**
- p99 latency requirements stricter than G1's 200ms target — algorithmic trading, real-time bidding, ad tech
- Very large heaps where G1's mixed collection pauses become significant
- After diagnosing that GC pauses are the dominant tail latency contributor, not a guess

In an interview, I'd emphasize the diagnostic step — measure first, switch second. ZGC is a real improvement, but it is not free, and chasing it without data wastes CPU.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
GC tuning in Java follows a strict discipline: measure first, diagnose second, change one flag at a time. Without baseline telemetry from GC logs, you're guessing — and changing heap sizes or GC algorithms without data typically makes things worse, not better.

**Step 1 — Enable GC logging:**
- `-Xlog:gc*` on Java 9+ — negligible overhead; provides all the telemetry needed for tuning decisions

**Step 2 — Distinguish minor GC from full GC:**
- Minor GC: reclaims young generation; typically 10-50ms; normal and expected
- Full GC: stops all application threads; can take seconds on large heaps; causes p99 latency spikes visible to users

**Diagnosing frequent full GC:**
- Post-GC live set stable but heap fills quickly → heap undersized; increase `-Xmx`
- Live set grows steadily over hours → memory leak; capture heap dump for analysis
- Sporadic full GC with no heap pressure → explicit `System.gc()` from monitoring agent or RMI; add `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`

I recommend always pairing GC logging with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` — when OOM strikes, you need the snapshot immediately rather than scrambling to reproduce after a restart.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
ZGC and Shenandoah achieve sub-millisecond pauses by performing **all** GC work — including compaction — concurrently with application threads.

ZGC (Oracle, production-ready in Java 15) uses **colored pointers** and load barriers to relocate objects without stopping the world.

Shenandoah (Red Hat, production-ready in Java 15) uses **Brooks pointers** (forwarding pointers in object headers) for the same goal. Both target heaps from a few hundred MB to multiple TB with pauses under 10ms — and typically under 1ms. The trade-off is 5-15% additional CPU overhead and modest extra memory for the relocation metadata. Use them when p99 latency requirements are stricter than what G1's `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` can deliver.

Saying GC works on reference counting (it does not — that's Python's CPython implementation; Java uses tracing collectors that walk from GC roots)

sections.title: Enable Logging, Read the Output, and Identify the Pause Pattern
sections.content:
The diagnostic workflow starts with enabling GC logging using the unified logging framework available in Java 9 and later.

```bash
java \
  -Xmx4g -Xms4g \
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/var/dumps/ \
  -jar app.jar
```

Each GC event produces a structured log line showing the collection type, heap before and after, and pause duration. A normal young GC entry looks like `GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) 512M->480M(4096M) 8.2ms` — the 8ms pause is healthy. A full GC entry like `GC(43) Pause Full (Ergonomics) 3800M->1200M(4096M) 1850ms` signals a problem worth investigating.

Upload the log file to **GCEasy** (web-based analyzer) or open it in **GraalVM Mission Control** for visual correlation of pause times, allocation rates, and heap occupancy trends. Look for three patterns: **steadily increasing live set after full GC** (memory leak), **frequent promotion failures** (old generation undersized relative to the allocation rate), and **explicit GC events** triggered by `System.gc()` calls from libraries or monitoring agents. For the last case, adding `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC` prevents external code from forcing stop-the-world pauses.

sections.title: Minor GC Is Healthy — Full GC Is the One You Worry About
sections.content:
In a healthy Java application, **minor GCs run constantly** — every few seconds in a busy web service — and you never notice them. Each minor GC reclaims the young generation in 10-50ms, well below any user-visible latency threshold. They are fast because the weak generational hypothesis holds: most young objects are dead by the time the GC scans them, so the work scales with the few survivors, not the entire heap.

**Full GC is the event you care about**. A full GC stops every application thread and walks the entire heap — young generation, old generation, and (in older JVMs) the Metaspace. On a 4GB heap, a full GC can take 1-3 seconds; on a 32GB heap, 10-30 seconds is not uncommon. These pauses are directly visible to users as p99 latency spikes, dropped requests, or — in distributed systems — false-positive failure detection by health checkers.

The terminology is sometimes confusing because **major GC** has slightly different meanings depending on the collector. In CMS and Parallel GC, a major GC means an old-generation collection. In G1, the equivalent is a **mixed GC**, which collects the young generation plus a few old-generation regions chosen by the garbage-density heuristic. In ZGC and Shenandoah, the distinction blurs because almost all collection work is concurrent.

The pragmatic interview-relevant view: any GC event labeled "Full" in the logs is a problem worth investigating. Any non-full event is part of normal operation.

sections.title: Minor vs Major vs Full GC — Scope, Cost, and Log Markers
sections.content:
Each GC type targets different parts of the heap with different costs and triggers.

| GC Type | What It Collects | Typical Pause | Triggered By | Log Marker (Java 9+) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minor GC | Young generation (Eden + active Survivor) | 10-50ms | Eden fills | `Pause Young (Normal)` |
| Major GC (CMS/Parallel) | Old generation | 100ms-seconds | Old gen occupancy threshold | `Pause Old` (rare in modern collectors) |
| Mixed GC (G1) | Young gen + a few old gen regions | 50-200ms | G1 garbage-density heuristic | `Pause Mixed` |
| Full GC | Entire heap (young + old + Metaspace) | Seconds | Promotion failure, Metaspace OOM, explicit `System.gc()` | `Pause Full` |

**Minor GC** is triggered when Eden fills. The collector copies live objects to the empty Survivor space (or promotes them to old gen if their age has reached the tenuring threshold) and reclaims Eden. The cost is proportional to the live data, which is typically a small fraction of Eden.

**G1's mixed GC** is the modern replacement for traditional major GC. Instead of collecting the entire old generation in one shot, G1 picks a few old-gen regions per cycle based on garbage density — the regions with the most garbage are evacuated first. This spreads the work across many small pauses rather than one large one, keeping pause times within the soft target.

**Full GC** is the event that breaks SLAs. It always stops the world, scans the entire heap, and compacts everything. In G1 specifically, a full GC means G1 has fallen back to a single-threaded serial collector — a sign that something has gone wrong with normal incremental collection. Common triggers:

- **Promotion failure** — survivors cannot fit in the Survivor space and old gen is too full to accept them.
- **To-space exhausted** (G1) — no fresh region available for evacuation.
- **Metaspace OOM** — class metadata exhausts the Metaspace; common in apps that load classes dynamically.
- **Explicit `System.gc()`** — a library, framework, or monitoring agent calls it.
- **`jcmd <pid> GC.run`** — a manual diagnostic trigger.

sections.title: Reading a GC Log — What Each Line Means
sections.content:
GC log analysis is the single most useful diagnostic skill for Java performance. The Java 9+ unified logging format is structured and easy to read once you know the markers.

**A healthy minor GC entry:**

```
[2026-04-23T10:15:32.123+0000][2.345s][info][gc] GC(42) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 512M->480M(4096M) 8.2ms
```

Decoded:
- `GC(42)` — 42nd GC since JVM start
- `Pause Young (Normal)` — minor GC, no anomalies
- `G1 Evacuation Pause` — G1's standard young-gen evacuation
- `512M->480M(4096M)` — heap before → after, total heap size
- `8.2ms` — pause duration

**A healthy G1 mixed GC:**

```
[2026-04-23T10:20:45.456+0000][312.456s][info][gc] GC(78) Pause Mixed (G1 Mixed GC) 3200M->1100M(4096M) 145ms
```

Decoded:
- `Pause Mixed` — G1's incremental old-gen collection
- 3200MB → 1100MB — significant memory reclaimed; healthy
- 145ms — within the default 200ms pause target

**An unhealthy full GC:**

```
[2026-04-23T10:30:12.789+0000][878.789s][info][gc] GC(99) Pause Full (G1 Evacuation Pause) (To-space exhausted) 4090M->3800M(4096M) 1850ms
```

Decoded:
- `Pause Full` — full GC; bad
- `(To-space exhausted)` — G1 ran out of fresh regions for evacuation
- 4090MB → 3800MB — only 290MB reclaimed; live set is growing or heap is undersized
- 1850ms — 1.8 second pause; will violate any latency SLA

The diagnostic pattern: **if `Pause Full` appears more than once or twice per day in production logs, you have a problem worth investigating**. The qualifier in parentheses tells you the trigger:

- `(System.gc())` — find and remove the explicit call (or set `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`)
- `(To-space exhausted)` — increase heap or `-XX:G1ReservePercent`
- `(Metadata GC Threshold)` — investigate Metaspace usage; raise `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`
- `(Allocation Failure)` — heap is undersized for the allocation rate
- `(Last ditch collection)` — JVM is about to throw OOM

sections.title: Preventing Full GC — Practical Mitigations by Trigger
sections.content:
Most full GCs are preventable once you know the trigger. Here are the common causes and the specific mitigations.

**Trigger: Explicit `System.gc()` calls.**
- Source: monitoring agents, RMI's distributed GC, libraries that call GC defensively.
- Mitigation: `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC` to ignore all explicit calls, or `-XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent` to convert them to a concurrent G1 cycle instead of a stop-the-world full GC.

**Trigger: Promotion failure / To-space exhausted.**
- Source: allocation rate exceeds what minor GC can promote; old gen has no headroom.
- Mitigation: increase `-Xmx`, increase `-XX:G1ReservePercent` (default 10%), or reduce allocation rate in application code.

**Trigger: Metaspace OOM.**
- Source: dynamic class loading without unloading; common with hot-reloading frameworks, scripting languages on the JVM, or repeated class generation by libraries like Mockito or CGLIB.
- Mitigation: set `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m` to bound it, monitor with JFR, fix any ClassLoader leaks.

**Trigger: Genuine memory leak.**
- Source: static collections growing forever, listeners never removed, `ThreadLocal` in pooled threads.
- Mitigation: capture a heap dump with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`, analyze with Eclipse MAT, fix the leak.

**Trigger: Heap simply undersized.**
- Source: live data set grew over time as the application scaled.
- Mitigation: increase `-Xmx`; this is the legitimate case where adding memory is the right answer.

**Anti-pattern to avoid:** calling `System.gc()` from application code to "clean up" before a critical operation. Modern collectors decide better than you can; explicit calls usually trigger expensive full GCs that hurt rather than help. The one exception is in long-running batch jobs where you genuinely want to compact between phases.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Minor GC** — collects young gen (Eden + Survivor); typically 10-50ms; normal and expected.
- **Major GC** — historically meant old-gen collection; in G1, called **mixed GC** and runs incrementally.
- **Full GC** — collects entire heap; stops all threads; seconds-long pauses; always investigate.
- **Java 9+ log markers** — `Pause Young`, `Pause Mixed`, `Pause Full`.
- **Common full GC triggers** — promotion failure, to-space exhausted, Metaspace OOM, explicit `System.gc()`.
- **`-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`** — silences `System.gc()` calls from libraries and monitoring agents.
- **`-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`** — always pair with GC logging in production.
- **GCEasy** and **GraalVM Mission Control** — for visual analysis of GC log patterns.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java garbage collection events fall into three categories, and being able to distinguish them in logs is essential for diagnosing production performance problems.

**Minor GC:**
- Collects the young generation — Eden plus the active Survivor space
- Typically 10-50ms — normal and expected; happens every few seconds in busy apps
- Triggered when Eden fills
- Log marker in Java 9+: `Pause Young (Normal)`

**Major GC (or Mixed GC in G1):**
- Targets the old generation
- In G1, it's incremental — `Pause Mixed` collects young gen plus a few old-gen regions per cycle
- Pause typically 50-200ms — within G1's `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` target
- Triggered by old-gen occupancy heuristics

**Full GC:**
- Collects the entire heap — young, old, and Metaspace
- Stops all application threads — pauses can take seconds on large heaps
- Causes visible p99 latency spikes and can trigger false-positive failure detection in distributed systems
- Log marker: `Pause Full` with a reason in parentheses

**Common full GC triggers and mitigations:**
- Explicit `System.gc()` from libraries — use `-XX:+DisableExplicitGC`
- Promotion failure or to-space exhausted in G1 — increase heap or `G1ReservePercent`
- Metaspace OOM — bound it with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` and fix the ClassLoader leak
- Genuine memory leak — capture a heap dump with `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` and analyze in Eclipse MAT

**The diagnostic discipline:**
- Always enable GC logging in production: `-Xlog:gc*` on Java 9+
- Treat minor GC as background noise; investigate every full GC
- Use GCEasy or Mission Control for visual analysis
- Pair GC logging with heap dump on OOM so you have the snapshot when things go wrong

In an interview, I'd emphasize that knowing how to read a GC log is more practical than memorizing GC algorithm internals — the log tells you what is actually happening in production.
